notes.title: Start here: DeskPilot, a support-ticket app on one JSON file
notes.body:
DeskPilot (in `deskpilot-clean/`) is a support-ticket web app: agents create tickets, move them through statuses, post public replies or internal notes, and read a per-ticket timeline. Customers use a portal link to submit and reply. It is Next.js with TypeScript and **no database**: all data lives in one JSON file that the store reads and rewrites.

Suggested reading order:

1. `_learning/00-ARCHITECTURE.md`: what exists, what is only a stub, and the data flow.
2. `_learning/01-LEARNING-PATH.md`, chapter by chapter. Chapters 1 (domain types and rules) and 2 (persistence) cover everything in this pack. Its lab setup lets you run the store with plain Node.
3. The per-file guides in `_learning/guides/src/lib/`, especially `state-machine.ts.guide.md` and `store.ts.guide.md`.
4. `_learning/03-PATTERNS.md`, whose findings section reports real, reproducible bugs.

Every quiz in this pack is about `src/lib/state-machine.ts` or `src/lib/store.ts`. Read each function with a small concrete example and predict its exact output.

excerpts.quote: DeskPilot is a support-ticket web app. Agents create tickets, change status, post public replies or internal notes, and read a per-ticket timeline.
All data lives in one JSON file, `data/deskpilot.json`, created from `src/lib/seed-data.ts` on first read

notes.title: The ticket state machine
notes.body:
A **state machine** is a fixed list of states plus the moves allowed between them. In DeskPilot the states are ticket statuses (open, in_progress, waiting_on_customer, blocked, resolved, closed), and `state-machine.ts` holds a `rules` table: for each status, the list of statuses it may move to.

`transitionTicket` is the only function that should change a status. Read it as a sequence of guards, in order: is there a ticket? is it merged? is the requested status the same as now? is the move in the table? Each guard either throws a `TransitionError`, returns early, or lets the next one run. Only after all of them does it change the status and log an event.

When you study the table, look for statuses that never appear as a *target* (so you can never get back to them), and for which store functions the transition calls. Both lead to quiz questions.

readMore.why: Guide to the transition rules and guards.

notes.title: Read, change, write: how the JSON store works
notes.body:
Every store function follows the same three steps: `readDb()` loads and parses the whole JSON file, the function changes the object in memory, and `writeDb(db)` serialises the whole object back to the file. There is no transaction and no partial update: each write replaces the entire file with that caller's copy.

`writeDb` chains writes through a module-level promise called `writeQueue`, so two file writes never overlap. Read the patterns guide's first finding carefully: it explains precisely what that chain protects and what it does not. The store guide's "common mistakes" list says the same thing from a different angle.

Other habits worth noticing in `store.ts`: every query filters by `orgId` (separate organizations share one file), and most changes push a row into `ticketEvents` so the timeline can show what happened. Check, for each function, whether the event is written always or only when something really changed.

excerpts.quote: Forgetting org filter, causing cross-tenant leakage.

readMore.why: The findings section: reproducible bugs with evidence.

notes.title: What addComment escapes, and what it leaves alone
notes.body:
The key is right: the body is trimmed, and only the less-than and greater-than signs are escaped. `addComment` first does `input.body.trim()`, removing the outer spaces. Then it builds `bodyHtml` by wrapping the text in a paragraph tag after `.replaceAll("<", "<").replaceAll(">", ">")`. So the `b` tag becomes `<b>` and cannot be read as HTML, but the ampersand in "Tom & Jerry" is left exactly as it is: nothing replaces `&`.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Only the ampersand escaped": the code never touches `&`, and it does escape the angle brackets.
- "Stored exactly as sent": the trim and both replacements run.
- "Every HTML special escaped": only two characters are replaced; `&` and quotes pass through.

notes.title: What happens to a merged ticket
notes.body:
The key is right: a merged ticket can no longer transition, and `listTickets` hides it. Two separate lines do this. In `transitionTicket`, right after finding the ticket, `if (ticket.isMerged)` throws `TransitionError("Merged tickets cannot transition.")`. In `listTickets`, the filter returns false for any ticket that is merged, so it never appears in the list. The record itself is not removed from the file; it just stops being visible or movable.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Can still go to closed": the merged check comes before any rule lookup and refuses every move.
- "Moves together with its target": nothing links the two tickets' statuses.
- "Deleted at merge time": the list filter would not be needed if it were deleted; the record stays.

excerpts.quote: if (ticket.isMerged) { throw new TransitionError("Merged tickets cannot transition.");

notes.title: Counting the reads and writes in one transition
notes.body:
The key is right: 3 reads and 2 writes. `transitionTicket` calls three store functions, and each one does its own read-modify-write:

- `getTicketById` calls `readDb()` and only returns the ticket: 1 read.
- `setTicketStatus` calls `readDb()`, changes the status, then `writeDb(db)`: 1 read, 1 write.
- `addTransitionEvent` calls `readDb()`, pushes the event, then `writeDb(db)`: 1 read, 1 write.

Total: 3 and 2. Because the status change and its event are two separate writes, a failure between them leaves a changed status with no audit event.

Why the others are wrong:
- "1 and 1 in a transaction": there are no transactions in this store.
- "2 and 1, one shared write": status and event are written by different functions.
- "3 and 3": `getTicketById` only reads.

excerpts.quote: export async function getTicketById(orgId: string, ticketId: string): Promise

notes.title: Why moving blocked to blocked does nothing
notes.body:
The key is right: the ticket is returned unchanged, with no write and no event. `transitionTicket` checks `if (ticket.status === input.nextStatus) return ticket;` **before** it looks at the rules table. So a request to move a ticket to the status it already has returns straight away: `setTicketStatus` and `addTransitionEvent` never run, so nothing is written and nothing is logged. Repeating the same request is harmless.

Why the others are wrong:
- "updatedAt bumped and saved": that would need `setTicketStatus`, which is not reached.
- "Rewritten and a blocked -> blocked event logged": the event is only written after the early return point.
- "TransitionError because blocked is not in its own list": true that blocked is not in its own list, but the same-status check returns before the list is consulted.

notes.title: How the next ticket number is chosen
notes.body:
The key is right: 8, the org's own highest number plus one. `nextTicketNumber` first filters tickets to the given `orgId`, then reduces them with `Math.max(acc, ticket.ticketNumber)` starting from 0, and returns that maximum plus 1. Org B's tickets are filtered out before the maximum is taken, so they do not matter. Org A's highest is 7, so the next is 8. (An org with no tickets gets 1.)

Why the others are wrong:
- "38, total count plus one": the code takes a maximum, not a count, and only within one org.
- "31, numbers shared across orgs": the org filter separates them.
- "UUID-derived": the ticket's `id` is a UUID, but `ticketNumber` comes from this function.

excerpts.quote: .filter((ticket) => ticket.orgId === orgId) .reduce((acc, ticket) => Math.max(acc, ticket.ticketNumber), 0); return max + 1;

notes.title: How updateTicketFields cleans a tag list
notes.body:
The key is right: `["vip", "billing"]`, trimmed, empties dropped, de-duplicated, in original order. The line is `Array.from(new Set(input.tags.map((tag) => tag.trim()).filter(Boolean)))`. Step by step: trim gives `["vip", "vip", "", "billing"]`; `filter(Boolean)` removes the empty string, giving `["vip", "vip", "billing"]`; a `Set` keeps only the first of each value **in the order it first appeared**, giving `["vip", "billing"]`. There is no sort.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Sorted": nothing sorts; a Set keeps insertion order.
- "Only the empty tag dropped": trimming happens first, so " vip" becomes "vip" and then the duplicate is removed.
- "Stored exactly as sent": all three cleanup steps run whenever `tags` is an array.

notes.title: Why two concurrent creates can lose a ticket
notes.body:
The key is right: only one ticket may survive, because each call writes its own full copy and the later write erases the other. Both calls run `readDb()` before either writes, so both start from the same file contents. Each adds its own ticket to *its own* copy and calls `writeDb(db)`, which writes the whole object. `writeQueue` makes the two writes happen one after the other, but the second simply replaces the file with a copy that never contained the first ticket. Both also computed the same `ticketNumber`. The patterns guide's Finding 1 reproduces this with five calls: all succeed, one is saved.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Both saved with one number": the file keeps only the last copy.
- "writeQueue serialises the cycles": it orders the file writes, not the read-change-write cycle.
- "The second write detects a conflict": there is no conflict check.

excerpts.quote: but each queued write is a full snapshot taken *before* the other requests' changes:
Five concurrent `createTicket` calls all return success with `ticketNumber: 1007`, and only one ticket is persisted.

notes.title: What reopening does to resolvedAt
notes.body:
The key is right: it keeps the old timestamp, because nothing ever clears `resolvedAt`. `setTicketStatus` sets the new status, then `if (input.status === "resolved" || input.status === "closed")` sets `resolvedAt` to now. For any other status (like `in_progress`) that branch is skipped, and there is no `else` that resets the field. So a reopened ticket still carries the time it was resolved, and a report could treat an in-progress ticket as resolved.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Set to the reopen time": only `updatedAt` is set on every change; `resolvedAt` is only set for resolved or closed.
- "Cleared to null": no line does that.
- "Moved into reopenedAt": no such field exists.

excerpts.quote: ticket.status = input.status; if (input.status === "resolved" || input.status === "closed") { ticket.resolvedAt = nowIso(); } ticket.updatedAt = nowIso();

notes.title: Which comment sets firstResponseAt
notes.body:
The key is right: the agent's public reply, the first comment that is both from an agent and not internal. The condition in `addComment` is `!ticket.firstResponseAt && input.authorType === "agent" && !input.isInternal`. Walk through the three comments:

- The internal note: agent, but `isInternal` is true, so it does not count.
- The customer's comment: `authorType` is "customer", so it does not count.
- The agent's public reply: agent and public, and the field is still empty, so it is set.

After that, `!ticket.firstResponseAt` is false, so later replies never move it.

Why the others are wrong:
- "The customer's comment": customers cannot set a *response* time.
- "The internal note": internal notes are excluded.
- "Only by a status transition": the field is set in `addComment`; `setTicketStatus` never touches it.

notes.title: What an update with unchanged fields still does
notes.body:
The key is right: `updatedAt` is bumped and the file rewritten, but no `ticket.updated` event is logged. Each field check compares the input with the current value and only records a change when they differ, so with the same subject and priority `newValue` stays empty. But `ticket.updatedAt = nowIso()` runs unconditionally after the checks, and `await writeDb(db)` runs at the end either way. The event push is the only step guarded by `Object.keys(newValue).length > 0`. Side effect: the ticket jumps to the top of any list sorted by `updatedAt`.

Why the others are wrong:
- "An event with no changed fields": the guard prevents an empty event.
- "A validation error": nothing requires a change.
- "Nothing at all, returns early": there is no early return for "no changes".

notes.title: Where a closed ticket may go
notes.body:
The key is right: only to `in_progress`. In the rules table, `closed: ["in_progress"]`. A closed ticket can be reopened into active work, and that is all. It cannot go to resolved, blocked, waiting, or open. In fact no status lists `open` as a target anywhere in the table, so open is only ever a starting status.

Why the others are wrong:
- "open or in_progress": `open` is not in closed's list (or anyone's).
- "Any status except closed": the list has exactly one entry.
- "None, closed is terminal": the list is not empty; reopening is allowed.
